result.text: The paper tackles how to train agents that can learn new sequential decision-making tasks from only a few demonstrations—i.e., achieve in-context learning—despite the extra challenges of stochastic, potentially irrecoverable environments. The key insight is that transformers will only acquire useful in-context learning for decision problems if they are trained on trajectory sequences with particular distributional properties (diversity, stochasticity, and bursty, multi-task coverage), and that model and dataset scale amplify this ability. The method is to empirically analyze design choices using an illustrative failure case, then train large transformer models on large, diverse offline datasets of trajectories with controlled task diversity, environment randomness, and trajectory burstiness, demonstrating few-shot generalization to new MiniHack and Procgen tasks without any weight updates.

The paper tackles the challenge of making vision-language models broadly useful by applying instruction tuning—an approach proven in NLP—to the more complex, multimodal setting where diverse visual inputs and tasks complicate generalization. The key insight is that assembling a large, diverse collection of vision-language datasets into a unified instruction-following format and equipping the model with an instruction-aware Query Transformer to extract task-relevant visual features enables much better zero-shot and fine-tuned performance. Methodologically, the authors convert 26 public VL datasets into instruction-tuning examples, train variants of BLIP-2 with the new Query Transformer on a subset of these datasets, and evaluate on 13 held-out sets, showing state-of-the-art zero-shot results and strong downstream fine-tuning gains compared to BLIP-2 and larger contemporaries; they open-source the resulting InstructBLIP models and code.

The paper addresses the vulnerability that machine unlearning systems—designed to efficiently remove a user’s data from trained models instead of retraining from scratch—can be forced to incur the full retraining cost, undermining practical guarantees and denial-of-service resistance. Its key insight is that certification formalisms for unlearning often ignore computational budgets, creating an attack surface where carefully crafted training examples (poisoning points) can be made pivotal so that any subsequent removal request for them forces the unlearning mechanism to fall back to expensive retraining. The authors formalize this attack objective, construct poisoning strategies that maximize the likelihood a point becomes influential enough to trigger retraining under common certified unlearning schemes, and empirically validate on standard datasets that small, targeted perturbations in training data substantially increase the rate of full retraining events, thereby demonstrating a realistic and efficient denial-of-service vector against certified machine unlearning.

The paper tackles semantic image segmentation conditioned on arbitrary natural-language labels, aiming to generalize to unseen categories without retraining. Its key insight is to align per-pixel image embeddings with text embeddings from a pretrained text encoder so that semantically related words map to similar regions in embedding space, enabling zero-shot label grounding. The method uses a transformer-based image encoder to produce dense pixel embeddings and trains it with a contrastive objective against text embeddings of class labels, yielding a single model that performs competitive zero- and few-shot segmentation and matches traditional supervised methods when given a fixed label set.

The paper addresses the problem of producing meaningful class labels for unlabeled video datasets without human annotation, noting that strong feature encoders alone do not yield usable pseudo-labels for videos. Its key insight is that the natural correspondence between audio and visual streams in videos provides a powerful self-supervisory signal that can guide clustering toward semantically coherent groups. The authors propose a multi-modal clustering method that jointly leverages audio-visual correspondence to assign pseudo-labels from scratch, and they validate that these clusters align well with human ground-truth categories. They also present the first benchmarks for unsupervised video labelling on Kinetics, Kinetics-Sound, VGG-Sound and AVE, with extensive analysis demonstrating strong semantic overlap with annotated labels.

The paper tackles the inefficiency of vision transformers by recognizing that final predictions depend on a small subset of informative tokens, so processing all tokens throughout the network is wasteful. The key insight is to dynamically and progressively prune redundant tokens per input using a lightweight importance-prediction module inserted at multiple layers, exploiting self-attention so that removed tokens can be masked out without harming differentiable training or hardware efficiency. Concretely, the method trains tiny token-scoring heads end-to-end with an attention-masking strategy that blocks pruned tokens’ interactions, hierarchically sparsifies up to ~66% of tokens, and thereby reduces FLOPs and increases throughput with minimal accuracy loss, producing competitive complexity/accuracy trade-offs on ImageNet.

The paper addresses the lack of convergence guarantees and sample complexity results for stochastic gradient methods with momentum when applied to constrained, non-smooth, non-convex optimization problems. Its key insight is that a carefully constructed Lyapunov function tailored to a Polyak-type momentum term enables provable convergence rates without requiring tuning of the momentum parameter. Methodologically, the authors analyze a stochastic subgradient method augmented with Polyak momentum for a broad class of non-smooth, non-convex, constrained problems, derive complexity bounds via the Lyapunov construction, and extend and sharpen existing bounds for smooth and unconstrained settings under weaker assumptions. Numerical experiments validate that the theoretical rates reflect practical behavior.

The paper addresses the gap between energy-efficient neuromorphic computing and emerging Transformer-based spiking neural networks (SNNs), where existing neuromorphic chips and CNN-based SNNs dominate but lack designs optimized for spike-driven Transformers and do not yield clear advantages. The key insight is that a meta-architectural reformulation of Spike-driven Transformers—carefully designing spike-driven self-attention, skip connections, and overall structure—can yield a versatile, low-power, spike-only-addition paradigm that outperforms CNN-style SNNs across vision tasks and can guide future neuromorphic chip design. Methodologically, the authors extend a prior Spike-driven Transformer into a Meta-SpikeFormer family, systematically exploring architectural choices and training directly on ImageNet-1K and downstream detection/segmentation tasks to demonstrate scalability and generality, achieving 80.0% top-1 accuracy (55M) and state-of-the-art SNN results while discussing implications for next-generation neuromorphic hardware.

The paper addresses how to learn identifiable causal generative models from observational data using flexible neural density estimators, and how to use them for interventions and counterfactuals even with mixed discrete-continuous variables and partial graph knowledge. The key insight is that recent non-linear ICA identifiability results imply that, given a causal ordering, autoregressive normalizing flows can recover the true causal conditionals and thus the causal model from observational data. The authors propose design and training guidelines for "causal normalizing flows" (autoregressive NFs tailored to causal graphs), show how to implement the do-operator within this framework to answer interventional and counterfactual queries, and validate their choices through ablations and comparisons on synthetic and real-world tasks.

The paper addresses point cloud panoptic segmentation, aiming to jointly produce semantic labels and instance groupings for 3D points without costly hand-crafted instance heuristics. Its key insight is that instance grouping can be learned end-to-end by a fixed set of point-level classifiers trained with a matching objective, eliminating the need for clustering, anchors, or NMS. The proposed PUPS method uses bipartite matching during training so classifiers exclusively predict instance groupings, refines predictions with a transformer decoder, and applies a context-aware CutMix augmentation to mitigate class imbalance; this simple unified approach yields state-of-the-art results on SemanticKITTI and nuScenes.

result.text: This paper addresses the problem of certifying robustness of machine learning models against data poisoning attacks that modify, delete, or insert training examples. The key insight is that bagging’s subsampling and majority-vote structure provides intrinsic, algorithm-agnostic resilience: if the number of poisoned training points is below a derived threshold, the ensemble’s majority vote cannot be flipped regardless of the base learner’s behavior. result.text: This paper addresses the security risk that machine unlearning—designed to remove specific data from trained models—can be abused to implant backdoors, so that the unlearned model misbehaves in the presence of a trigger. The key insight is that selectively removing particular contributed examples (or combining minor upfront poisoning with later unlearning) can shift model decision boundaries in a controlled way, enabling backdoor activation without obvious tampering of the original training set. The authors propose two attack methods: a pure-unlearning attack that achieves a backdoor solely by submitting malicious unlearning requests for a small subset of the attacker’s contributed data, and a hybrid attack that first plants a few poisoned examples with a trigger and then activates the backdoor via unlearning; both optimize attack utility while maintaining stealth. result.text: The paper addresses the high computational cost of vision transformers (ViTs), particularly the quadratic scaling with token count and limitations of existing token-reduction methods that either break spatial structure or require costly pretraining. Its key insight is to perform dynamic, instance-wise token selection using the transformer’s native global class attention and then treat retained (“informative”) and dropped (“uninformative”) tokens differently through a slow-fast updating scheme that preserves spatial structure and information flow. The method, called Evo-ViT, selects tokens via class-attention-based scoring and routes selected tokens through more frequent, heavier updates while routing unselected tokens through lighter, less frequent updates, enabling compatibility with both flat and deep-narrow ViT architectures from training start. Experiments show Evo-ViT greatly reduces FLOPs and increases throughput (e.g., >60% speedup on DeiT-S) with minimal accuracy loss (~0.4% top-1 on ImageNet-1K), outperforming prior pruning approaches in efficiency and accuracy.

result.text: The paper tackles zero-shot semantic segmentation using pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP, addressing the problem that prior methods only align text embeddings with the last-layer visual features and thus miss rich object detail in intermediate layers, while naive aggregation of multi-level features hurts alignment for novel classes. The key insight is that large discrepancies between features from different visual layers make direct multi-level fusion ineffective, so aligning each level to the text space independently but in a cascaded manner preserves discriminative detail without degrading zero-shot generalization. The method, Cascade-CLIP, attaches a series of independent decoders to intermediate network layers and aligns each decoder’s visual embeddings to CLIP text embeddings sequentially, producing cascaded vision-language alignments that can be plugged into existing zero-shot segmentation pipelines and which improve performance on COCO-Stuff, Pascal-VOC, and Pascal-Context.

result.text: The paper tackles causal representation learning when observations are only partially informative—each measurement reveals a subset of latent causal variables and the observable subset can vary per instance—challenging standard identifiability assumptions that all latents are always reflected in data. The key insight is that an instance-dependent sparsity pattern in how latents mix into observations provides a principled constraint that enables identifiability: under either linear mixing with minimal assumptions or piecewise-linear mixing with Gaussian latents, the true causal factors can be recovered. Methodologically, the authors derive two theoretical identifiability results and develop two corresponding estimation algorithms that encourage sparsity in the recovered representations to match the partial-observability structure. Empirical results on synthetic and benchmark datasets show these sparsity-enforcing methods more accurately recover ground-truth latent variables than prior approaches.

result.text: The paper addresses the shortage of high-quality instruction-tuning data for vision-language models, noting that existing pipelines using language-only generators (e.g., GPT-4) depend on pre-annotated captions and boxes and that current multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) are weaker and prone to hallucinations. The key insight is that accessible MLLMs can nonetheless be leveraged to create diverse vision-language instruction data if paired with an on-the-fly correction loop that detects and fixes generated inaccuracies, thereby mitigating hallucination and improving quality without requiring dense human annotation. The proposed VIGC framework combines Visual Instruction Generation (VIG), which steers MLLMs to produce varied instruction-response pairs from images, with Visual Instruction Correction (VIC), an iterative update mechanism that validates and refines those outputs to remove errors; the resulting synthetic dataset is used to fine-tune mainstream models. Experiments show that VIGC-generated data yields higher-quality training corpora than language-only approaches and improves benchmark performance, and the authors release models, data, and code.

The key insight is to aggregate ViT patch embeddings into semantic regions via a set of learnable center vectors that dynamically gather patches belonging to the same concept, enabling segmentation driven by text-image supervision. result.text: The paper tackles the high computational cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) at inference and training time by reducing the number of tokens processed without retraining or with minimal training. The key insight is that many tokens are redundant (e.g., multiple tokens representing parts of the same object or across frames) and can be merged into representative tokens with little accuracy loss, so selectively combining similar tokens yields large speedups. The proposed method, Token Merging (ToMe), uses a lightweight, general matching algorithm to pair and merge similar token embeddings during forward passes (optionally applied during training), thereby cutting token count and compute while preserving information; empirically ToMe doubles throughput for large ViTs on images, videos, and audio with only ~0.2–0.4% accuracy/mAP drops and can also accelerate MAE fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper studies the effect of gradient clipping—rescaling gradients whose norm exceeds a threshold c—on optimization, addressing gaps in prior convergence analyses that required special c choices or strong noise assumptions. The key insight is that clipping has limited impact in deterministic gradient descent (it only alters higher-order terms) but introduces a stochastic bias that can prevent convergence to the true optimum under standard noise models, so guarantees must explicitly depend on c and the noise structure. Methodologically, the authors derive tight upper and lower bounds for the convergence of the gradient norm for clipped SGD across arbitrary clipping thresholds, proving that deterministic guarantees are robust to clipping while stochastic settings admit unavoidable bias, and corroborate these theoretical findings with experiments.

result.text: The paper tackles the growing memory burden of key-value (KV) caches during decoding in autoregressive transformer LLMs, which becomes prohibitive at long sequence lengths and large batch sizes. Its key insight is that, beyond sharing key/value heads across query heads as in Multi-Query Attention (MQA) and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), adjacent transformer layers can also share key and value heads without materially harming accuracy. The authors propose Cross-Layer Attention (CLA), an attention block design that reuses KV heads across neighboring layers to halve the KV cache size relative to MQA, and they validate this by training 1B- and 3B-parameter models showing CLA achieves a Pareto improvement in the memory-versus-accuracy tradeoff. This enables inference with longer contexts and larger batches while maintaining near-MQA performance.

The paper addresses why existing causal representation learning methods fail to disentangle latent factors from multi-object observations, showing that the common assumptions of vector-valued latents and an injective generative map break down when scenes contain multiple interchangeable objects. The key insight is that object-centric inductive biases restore identifiability because representing each object with its own slot makes the generative mapping effectively injective over object properties, so sparse perturbations targeted to objects provide much stronger supervision for causal disentanglement than global Euclidean encodings. Methodologically, the authors modify the Slot Attention architecture to produce object-wise representations and train it with weak supervision from sparse interventions (perturbations) so that each slot learns disentangled properties; empirically this object-centric approach disentangles object attributes with far fewer perturbations than a comparable monolithic encoder in image-based experiments.

Its key insight is that applying masked autoencoding to state-action trajectories—randomly masking tokens and reconstructing them—forces the model to learn dynamics and infer missing states and actions, and that varying mask proportions improves generalization. result.text: The paper tackles the high cost and complexity of adapting large language models to vision-language tasks, where prior approaches require heavy parameter tuning and large-scale pretraining. The key insight is that lightweight adapters plus a routing mechanism can efficiently bridge an image encoder and an LLM, enabling joint optimization and automatic switching between unimodal and multimodal instruction contexts without degrading language understanding. The proposed Mixture-of-Modality Adaptation (MMA) inserts small adapter modules between the image encoder and LLaMA, uses a routing algorithm to determine modality mixing, and fine-tunes only a few million parameters while jointly training the vision and language components. Experiments on multimodal science QA and dialogue show that the resulting LaVIN model matches competitive performance of larger multimodal LLMs with far lower compute and training time (e.g., 3.8M trainable parameters and 1.4 hours).

The key insight is that when interventions (e.g., agent actions) are observable, one can jointly learn a mapping from observations to multidimensional causal variables and a causal graph that permits instantaneous effects, restoring identifiability in intervened sequences. result.text: The paper addresses open-vocabulary image segmentation in complex scenes where objects and regions naturally admit multiple levels of semantic granularity, which creates inherent ambiguity that prior methods largely ignore. Its key insight is that explicitly modeling a hierarchical representation spanning different semantic levels and treating “things” (countable objects) and “stuff” (amorphous regions) differently reduces ambiguity and improves generalization to novel labels. The method, called HIPIE, implements a decoupled text–image fusion and separate representation learning modules for things and stuff, systematically analyzing and adapting to their differing visual and textual feature characteristics, and integrates these components into a unified hierarchical open‑vocabulary segmentation framework. Evaluated across 40+ datasets covering semantic, instance, part, and referring tasks, HIPIE achieves state‑of‑the‑art results.

result.text: The paper tackles unsupervised discovery of robotic options (temporally-extended skills) from demonstration data, aiming to learn both low-level control policies and a higher-level policy that sequences them without task-specific supervision. The key insight is to represent options as continuous latent variables and cast option discovery as latent-variable inference over entire trajectories, exploiting a temporal factorization of trajectory likelihoods to capture how latent skills evolve and persist over time. Methodologically, the authors derive a temporal variational inference objective that decomposes trajectory likelihoods into temporally-structured terms, train encoder and decoder networks to infer and decode continuous option latents from demonstration sequences, and jointly optimize low-level option policies and a high-level usage policy. They validate the approach by demonstrating learned, reusable options across three robotic demonstration datasets.

The key insight is that feature representations of poisoned (triggered) samples are more sensitive to input transformations than clean samples, so measuring feature consistency towards transformations (FCT) reliably distinguishes poisoned from clean data. result.text: The paper addresses the problem of obtaining parameter-free high-probability regret guarantees for online convex optimization over unbounded domains when only heavy-tailed (finite p-th moment, p in (1,2]) subgradient estimates are available. The key insight is that standard martingale concentration and existing regularizers fail because iterates can grow exponentially in unbounded domains, so one must design regularization and control techniques that simultaneously tame large iterates and handle heavy-tailed noise to permit high-probability bounds. Concretely, the authors develop new regularizers and analysis that limit iterate growth and incorporate robust truncation/variance control to derive, with probability at most δ, a uniform regret bound of order Õ(∥u∥ T^{1/p} log(1/δ)) for every comparator u, matching parameter-free rates under only p-th moment assumptions.

result.text: The paper tackles the high computational and memory cost of training Transformers on long sequences by reducing attention and activation-storage bottlenecks. The key insight is that attention can be approximated with locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) to limit pairwise comparisons and that reversible residual layers eliminate the need to store intermediate activations for every layer. The method implements LSH-based attention to reduce attention complexity from O(L^2) to O(L log L) and replaces standard residual connections with reversible functions so activations are recomputed during the backward pass, yielding the Reformer architecture. Empirically, Reformers match standard Transformer performance while using far less memory and running much faster on long-sequence tasks.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of recovering time-delayed latent causal variables and their relations from observed temporal mixtures, a task made difficult because latent variables are generally not uniquely identifiable from nonlinear mixtures. The key insight is that temporal structure — specifically nonstationarity or parametric temporal dynamics — can provide sufficient constraints to identify temporally causal latent processes without relying on standard assumptions like sparsity or minimality. The authors introduce LEAP, a VAE-based framework that encodes these identifiability conditions into the causal-process prior and learning constraints, and they provide theoretical guarantees for two settings (nonparametric nonstationary and parametric) along with empirical evidence showing superior recovery of latent causal processes across varied datasets and dependency structures.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of scaling transformer-like architectures for 3D point cloud learning, where quadratic attention makes long sequences and resource-constrained deployment impractical. Its key insight is to adapt the RWKV sequence model to point clouds by combining a linear-time, recurrent attention mechanism with multi-headed matrix-valued states for global context while simultaneously capturing local geometry via a parallel fixed-radius neighbor graph and a graph stabilizer. The resulting PointRWKV is a multi-scale hierarchical framework that processes embedded point patches through modified PointRWKV blocks for global aggregation and a lightweight local branch for geometric encoding, enabling end-to-end hierarchical feature learning for downstream 3D tasks. Experiments show PointRWKV outperforms transformer and mamba baselines while reducing FLOPs by roughly 42%, offering an efficient alternative for building foundational 3D models.

result.text: The paper addresses the high computational cost of vision transformers (ViTs), particularly the quadratic scaling with token count and limitations of existing token-reduction methods that either break spatial structure or require costly pretraining. Its key insight is to perform dynamic, instance-wise token selection using the transformer’s native global class attention and then treat retained (“informative”) and dropped (“uninformative”) tokens differently through a slow-fast updating scheme that preserves spatial structure and information flow. The method, called Evo-ViT, selects tokens via class-attention-based scoring and routes selected tokens through more frequent, heavier updates while routing unselected tokens through lighter, less frequent updates, enabling compatibility with both flat and deep-narrow ViT architectures from training start. Experiments show Evo-ViT greatly reduces FLOPs and increases throughput (e.g., >60% speedup on DeiT-S) with minimal accuracy loss (~0.4% top-1 on ImageNet-1K), outperforming prior pruning approaches in efficiency and accuracy.

result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised pre-training for reinforcement learning: how to acquire useful behaviors and representations in reward-free environments so agents can rapidly learn downstream tasks once task rewards are introduced. The key insight is to drive exploration by maximizing a non-parametric estimate of entropy in an abstract representation space rather than in pixel space or via explicit density models, which sidesteps hard high-dimensional density estimation and produces diverse, semantically meaningful state coverage. The method, called APT, learns an abstract embedding of observations and uses a non-parametric entropy bonus computed from distances in that embedding to train an exploration policy during a long unsupervised phase; after pre-training the agent is fine-tuned on task rewards, yielding human-level or competitive performance on many Atari games and superior asymptotic performance and data efficiency on DMControl tasks.

result.text: The paper addresses learning rich self-supervised video representations from unlabelled audio-visual data, aiming to capture both modality-specific features and complementary cross-modal information despite domain discrepancies between audio and visual streams. The key insight is that combining masked-data reconstruction to learn strong modality-specific embeddings with a self-supervised teacher–student cross-modal knowledge distillation, augmented by a domain alignment strategy, enables effective transfer of complementary cues across modalities. The method trains two pseudo-objectives: (1) masked reconstruction on audio and visual inputs to build modality-tailored encoders, and (2) cross-modal knowledge distillation where a teacher from one modality guides a student in the other after aligning their feature domains, and it also proposes modality-agnostic variants that reuse a single pretrained backbone for both streams. Empirically, XKD yields substantial gains on action and sound classification benchmarks (e.g., +8–14% on UCF101/HMDB51/Kinetics400, +5.5% multimodal on Kinetics-Sound, and 96.5% on ESC50).

result.text: The paper addresses causal effect estimation from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounders, noting that standard front-door adjustment conditions are often too restrictive to hold in practice. Its key insight is to generalize front-door adjustment to a conditional front-door (CFD) criterion that relaxes those restrictions and to show that causal effects are identifiable under this weaker, more realistic condition. To operationalize CFD when the required mediator-like variable is not observed, the authors introduce CFDiVAE, an identifiable variational autoencoder that learns a CFD adjustment representation from data and comes with formal identifiability guarantees for the learned latent. Empirical results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate CFDiVAE’s effectiveness and robustness to the strength of unobserved confounding compared to existing methods.

args.text: We propose annealed clipping for normalized-momentum SGD in nonconvex problems with heavy-tailed or unbounded gradients: begin with aggressive norm clipping to prevent explosion, then raise the clipping threshold c_t according to a robust scale estimate (e.g., rolling high quantile or MAD) of recent gradient norms so that the clipping probability decays to zero. A Lyapunov analysis with time-varying clipping shows high-probability stability and last-iterate descent during burn-in, and asymptotic removal of clipping bias, yielding convergence to stationary points of the original (unclipped) objective. The scheme reconciles the stabilization benefits of clipping in non-Lipschitz regimes with the bias of fixed thresholds, while normalization+momentum eliminates sensitivity to batch size and unknown smoothness. We predict a two-phase rate—heavy-tail-robust during burn-in, then standard smooth nonconvex rates as c_t grows—and validate a parameter-free quantile schedule in practice.

result.text: The paper tackles long-context compression for transformer LLMs to reduce the high compute and memory costs of storing and attending to very long inputs. The key insight is to compress internal activations (keys and values) progressively at fine-grained input units rather than rely on external soft prompts, and to teach the model to produce and consume these compressed activations via a compression-aware training objective so the model itself learns to preserve task-relevant information across many compression ratios. Methodologically, the authors introduce Activation Beacon, a plug-in module that compresses layerwise KV activations with a progressive workflow, trains the model with compression-based auto-regression using plain text and instruction data while randomly sampling compression ratios per step, and evaluates on extreme-length tasks (up to 128K) to show comparable performance to uncompressed baselines with roughly 2× faster inference and an 8× reduction in KV memory.

args.text: PanopticStream: a streaming 3D panoptic segmentation model that maintains a recurrent bank of instance prototypes across frames and performs bipartite matching jointly against current point features and the memory to yield consistent IDs and improved masks. Building on end-to-end matching-based panoptic/instance grouping and prototypical labeling, we replace quadratic attention with a linear-time recurrent state to scale to long LiDAR sequences, and update prototypes with gated EMA and re-identification cues. We further inject a boundary-aware modulation that downweights cross-instance feature mixing near predicted borders and add a memory-consistency loss that enforces cycle-consistent prototype assignments over multi-frame clips. This yields online panoptic segmentation with lower ID switches and better boundary quality without hand-crafted tracking heuristics.

result.text: UniMASK tackles the problem of unifying diverse sequential decision-making tasks (e.g., behavior cloning, offline RL, inverse dynamics, waypoint conditioning) by framing them as different masking-and-prediction problems over sequences of states, actions, and returns. The key insight is that randomly masking elements of decision sequences and training a single model to predict the masked pieces can naturally express a wide range of control tasks as special cases of the same pretraining objective. The method defines a flexible masking scheme and trains a single transformer-style model on many such maskings so it can solve multiple tasks at inference time, and demonstrates that this unified model matches or exceeds single-task baselines and further improves with fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper addresses the limited open-ended task flexibility of current vision foundation models (VFMs), which are powerful but typically constrained to predefined task formats, unlike large language models (LLMs) that can handle diverse user-defined tasks via natural language. The key insight is to treat images as a “foreign language” and recast vision-centric problems as language-style tasks that an LLM-based decoder can interpret and execute according to flexible textual instructions. The method, called VisionLLM, aligns visual features with the LLM’s token space and uses the LLM as an open-ended decoder to produce task-specific outputs—from fine-grained object-level predictions to coarse task-level behaviors—guided solely by language prompts. Experiments demonstrate strong customization and competitive performance (e.g., >60% mAP on COCO) without task-specific detectors, suggesting a generalist LLM-centric paradigm for vision-and-language modeling.

result.text: This paper addresses the security risk that machine unlearning—designed to remove specific data from trained models—can be abused to implant backdoors, so that the unlearned model misbehaves in the presence of a trigger. The key insight is that selectively removing particular contributed examples (or combining minor upfront poisoning with later unlearning) can shift model decision boundaries in a controlled way, enabling backdoor activation without obvious tampering of the original training set. The authors propose two attack methods: a pure-unlearning attack that achieves a backdoor solely by submitting malicious unlearning requests for a small subset of the attacker’s contributed data, and a hybrid attack that first plants a few poisoned examples with a trigger and then activates the backdoor via unlearning; both optimize attack utility while maintaining stealth. They empirically validate these attacks across multiple unlearning algorithms, model architectures, and datasets, showing that unlearning mechanisms can be exploited to reliably and covertly insert backdoors.

Use these prototypes to supervise group tokens with a curriculum that first aligns tokens to coarse prototypes (stabilizing all-to-one training) and then to fine prototypes (bridging to one-to-one inference), while decoupling things vs. stuff pathways in a hierarchical open-vocabulary framework. The supervision is text-guided via cosine matching between text embeddings and diffusion-derived prototypes, yet remains label-efficient because no pixel masks are required. This should yield tighter, less redundant groupings and stronger zero-/few-shot generalization across domains.

result.text: The paper addresses the dual problem of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for vision transformers (ViTs) while also improving inference efficiency, which current PEFT methods largely neglect and which limits deployment of large pre-trained ViTs. The key insight is that many input tokens are less informative for a given task and can be dynamically identified and routed to skip expensive transformer blocks, so combining lightweight adapter modules with token-level dynamic skipping reduces redundant computation without harming adaptation quality. The proposed method, Dynamic Tuning (DyT), augments ViTs with a token dispatcher that classifies tokens as informative or skippable at each block, explores design variants for optimal dispatcher and adapter interaction, and incorporates a mixture-of-experts–inspired enhanced adapter to further boost performance. Experiments on image/video recognition and semantic segmentation show DyT matches or outperforms existing PEFT approaches while significantly cutting inference FLOPs (e.g., to 71% on VTAB-1K).

The key insight is that, under a linear generative model, diversity across domains (e.g., varying interventions or mixing) provides enough constraints to render the joint latent distribution and the shared causal graph identifiable from marginals alone. args.text: We propose Proto-Set Panoptic (PSP), a clustering-free 3D panoptic segmentation framework that unifies learned semantic/instance prototypes with set-predicted instance slots: class-conditioned prototypes provide interpretable anchors while a fixed-size set of instance queries is trained via bipartite matching to produce superpoint masks. Architecturally, a lightweight PointRWKV global-context backbone with a parallel local geometric branch feeds a prototype-conditioned decoder that attends over superpoints, while an auxiliary boundary-prediction head and boundary-aware aggregation sharpen instance borders. We pretrain prototypes and instance slots using large-scale 2D SAM-derived multi-view pseudo-masks fused into 3D, then finetune with true 3D labels; this yields scalable pretraining without manual 3D masks and improves generalization across indoor/outdoor scenes. PSP targets state-of-the-art panoptic quality with fewer heuristics than voting/clustering pipelines, plus natural extensibility to promptable or interactive use via prototype/slot conditioning.

args.text: We propose Clip-and-Correct Momentum (CCM) to reconcile the stability of gradient clipping with its stochastic bias: per-iteration, compute a mini-batch of gradients, apply general-norm clipping for stability, then perform a lightweight randomized self-normalization that debiases the clipped estimator by upweighting a small, Poisson-thinned subset of overly clipped samples, followed by a normalized momentum step. Under only bounded p-th moments (p in (1,2]), CCM controls variance on par with clipped-and-normalized schemes while eliminating the asymptotic bias of fixed-threshold clipping, yielding high-probability, last-iterate convergence to true ε-stationarity for smooth nonconvex objectives and extending to prox-constrained, nonsmooth settings via a Lyapunov analysis. A practical schedule increases the clipping threshold while decreasing the thinning rate, recovering monotone descent after a short warm-up and matching best-known heavy-tail-robust rates without sacrificing asymptotic correctness. Empirically, CCM should retain early-iterate stability, improve robustness to unbounded gradients, and close the gap to adaptive normalized momentum in heavy-tailed regimes.

args.text: CFD-SlotCRL: an identifiable object-centric causal representation learner for partially observed temporal data with unknown intervention targets. We learn latent mediators that satisfy the conditional front-door (CFD) criterion via an identifiable VAE whose encoder–decoder induces CFD-implied conditional independences and do-invariance constraints in the latent space, while a slot-based encoder and instance-dependent sparsity handle multi-object scenes and partial observability. Temporal nonstationarity and time-delay priors provide additional variation to disambiguate causality, and contrastive pairs across environments resolve unknown intervention targets; structural conditionals are parameterized by causal normalizing flows to enable exact interventional sampling and counterfactuals. We derive identifiability conditions combining CFD, partial-observation sparsity, and temporal variation, and demonstrate recovery of latent causal variables, their graph, and do-queries from raw video and multi-sensor streams.

We propose Prompt-Matched Dynamic Prototypes (PMDP) for streaming 3D panoptic segmentation: a scene-level prototype bank is maintained online, with bipartite matching assigning superpoint masks to prototypes each frame to enable birth/death events and enforce temporal consistency. The segmentation head follows a prototypical distance metric to unify semantic and instance granularity, while a superpoint-query decoder produces per-frame candidate masks that are efficiently matched to the evolving prototype set. Prototypes are initialized and optionally guided by 2D SAM-derived pseudo-masks and user prompts, enabling zero-shot and interactive refinement in cluttered or long-tail scenarios. Combined with context-aware augmentation, PMDP delivers promptable, temporally consistent panoptic outputs without heuristic clustering or NMS.

result.text: The paper tackles how to train agents that can learn new sequential decision-making tasks from only a few demonstrations—i.e., achieve in-context learning—despite the extra challenges of stochastic, potentially irrecoverable environments. The key insight is that transformers will only acquire useful in-context learning for decision problems if they are trained on trajectory sequences with particular distributional properties (diversity, stochasticity, and bursty, multi-task coverage), and that model and dataset scale amplify this ability. The method is to empirically analyze design choices using an illustrative failure case, then train large transformer models on large, diverse offline datasets of trajectories with controlled task diversity, environment randomness, and trajectory burstiness, demonstrating few-shot generalization to new MiniHack and Procgen tasks without any weight updates.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem that language-supervised semantic segmentation underperforms because image captions often omit many visual concepts, creating a semantic gap between visual content and paired text that weakens zero-shot dense prediction. Its key insight is to automatically enrich caption semantics by mining visually relevant concepts for each image using a pre-trained vision-language model (CLIP), thereby aligning textual supervision with the image's actual visual content. The proposed Concept Curation (CoCu) method builds a per-image concept archive via vision-driven expansion and text-to-vision-guided ranking, selects relevant concepts through cluster-guided sampling, and injects these concepts into pre-training so textual representations better reflect image semantics. Experiments on eight segmentation benchmarks show CoCu substantially improves zero-shot transfer and markedly boosts language-supervised segmentation baselines, demonstrating the benefit of closing the visual–textual semantic gap.

args.text: We propose Diffusion-Stepped Hierarchical Prototypical Regularization for weakly open-vocabulary segmentation: aggregate cross- and self-attention fields from a pretrained text-to-image diffusion U-Net across denoising steps to form a bank of non-learnable region prototypes, explicitly decoupled for things vs stuff. Group tokens are supervised to match these fixed prototypes, while a cascaded alignment attaches lightweight decoders at multiple visual levels to align embeddings to CLIP text, preserving fine detail and zero-shot generalization. High-confidence diffusion-derived regions bootstrap a self-training loop, and concept curation expands underspecified image–text pairs to improve label coverage. This diffusion-grounded, hierarchical scheme closes the train–test granularity gap and should improve zero-/few-shot and WOVSS across diverse domains.

result.text: The paper tackles learning visual correspondence from unlabeled video by framing correspondence as link prediction on a space-time graph whose nodes are image patches and temporally adjacent nodes can be connected by directed edges. The key insight is to learn patch embeddings that define transition probabilities for a random walk so that long-range correspondences are recovered as high-probability paths; training uses cycle-consistency as a self-supervised signal by maximizing the likelihood of returning to an initial node after walking along a palindrome of frames. Methodologically, they construct the graph from raw video, train an embedding network so pairwise similarities parameterize transition matrices, and optimize the probability of cycle-return via contrastive objectives; at test time they show improvements from self-supervised adaptation and stochastic edge dropout. The simple random-walk/contrastive formulation scales to large unlabeled video and outperforms prior self-supervised approaches on multiple label-propagation benchmarks for objects, parts, and pose.

args.text: We propose Residual-Clipped Normalized Momentum (RCNM), which augments clipped, normalized gradient methods with an error-feedback residual that accumulates the clipped-off gradient mass and re-injects a projection of this residual into future updates through the normalized momentum direction. By projecting the residual back onto the current clipping ball before accumulation (and slowly leaking it with a calibrated decay), RCNM cancels the bias introduced by clipping while preserving iterate stability, yielding last-iterate guarantees and heavy-tail robustness. Analytically, we show under p-th moment noise (p∈(1,2]) that RCNM attains the high-probability rates of normalized momentum methods without clipping-induced asymptotic bias and without tuning batch sizes, and we give an adaptive threshold schedule based on running quantiles of gradient norms that is parameter-free and avoids exponential smoothness sensitivity. This directly addresses the stochastic bias barrier of clipping and unifies the benefits of clipping, normalization, and momentum into a debiased, stable optimizer.

args.text: We propose Controllable Future Embeddings (CoFE), a pretraining-and-conditioning scheme that combines unsupervised future-embedding decision pretraining with an explicit dichotomy-of-control decomposition. During reward-free pretraining, a masked trajectory objective learns future embeddings while a mutual-information bottleneck partitions each future code into a controllable component (predictive of actions) and an exogenous component (correlated with environment stochasticity). At finetuning, we adopt PDT-style value assignment but only over the controllable code: a value head learns preferences on controllable embeddings, and the decision policy conditions solely on these targets while ignoring exogenous factors at inference. This yields conditioning consistency and robust behavior extraction in highly stochastic or irrecoverable settings, while retaining the benefits of large-scale, reward-free pretraining.

args.text: We propose Budgeted Active Tokenization for ViTs: casting token selection as a sequential decision process that explicitly maximizes expected value-of-information under a compute budget. The model starts with a coarse token grid and at each step uses a learned policy, conditioned on current token features and predictive uncertainty, to choose among split (refine a region), keep, merge, or drop actions for individual tokens; inference halts when confidence or budget criteria are met. Training combines imitation from a dense-teacher that provides per-region marginal loss-reduction targets with reinforcement learning whose reward is accuracy gain per FLOP, and the policy reuses token merging and slow/fast routing to maintain information flow. Compared to cascaded dynamic resolution and pruning methods, this yields foveated, interpretable compute allocation and improves the accuracy–latency Pareto on ImageNet and streaming video by adapting decisions across layers and frames.

args.text: We propose Cross-Layer Delta-KV: store full keys/values only at sparse anchor layers and reconstruct intermediate layers’ K/V via lightweight learned transforms from the nearest anchor while keeping a small, quantized residual per head. Training uses a compression-aware objective that randomly samples layer-group sizes and residual ranks/quantization and distills attention distributions so the model learns to attend correctly under reconstruction, while reversible blocks mitigate added training-time memory. At inference, this composes with cross-layer sharing by reusing K/V across neighboring layers but encoding them as deltas, plus an error-bounded refresh gate that recomputes exact K/V for tokens whose predicted attention mass exceeds a threshold. The design targets large KV cache reductions for long-context decoding and remains compatible with sparse-attention or efficient-attention backbones.

args.text: We propose Boundary-Conditioned Prototype Panoptic Segmentation (BCPPS), which unifies semantic, instance, and panoptic 3D point-cloud segmentation by injecting explicit boundary awareness into prototype learning and instance matching. A boundary head first predicts point-wise boundary probabilities to construct a boundary-weighted neighborhood graph and derive superpoints; a prototypical segmentation head then assigns class and instance labels using a boundary-conditioned distance metric that increases separation across high-probability boundaries while encouraging compactness within low-boundary regions. An instance set-prediction decoder operates on superpoints with boundary-masked attention and bipartite matching, eliminating post-hoc clustering and reducing cross-instance leakage at object borders. This synergy of boundary prediction, prototypical unification, and superpoint/matching paradigms improves near-boundary PQ and mIoU with minimal overhead.

This paper addresses the problem of certifying robustness of machine learning models against data poisoning attacks that modify, delete, or insert training examples. The key insight is that bagging’s subsampling and majority-vote structure provides intrinsic, algorithm-agnostic resilience: if the number of poisoned training points is below a derived threshold, the ensemble’s majority vote cannot be flipped regardless of the base learner’s behavior. The authors prove a tight bound on that threshold (tight when no assumptions are made about the base learner), derive a certification procedure that counts how many base models’ training sets would be affected by a given tampering budget, and empirically validate the approach on MNIST and CIFAR-10—reporting, for example, 91.1% certified accuracy on MNIST against arbitrary modifications/deletions/insertions of 100 training examples.

args.text: We propose Handover-Aware Visual Token Offloading: train MLLMs with explicit cross-layer handover mechanisms that transfer visual information into the text stream so visual tokens can be withdrawn adaptively and safely per instance. Starting from a dynamic tokenizer (e.g., semantic-equivalent or Matryoshka tokens), we attach lightweight handover auditors at successive layers that reconstruct discrete/continuous visual targets from only text-token states, and optimize a curriculum that masks/withdraws vision tokens once auditor error falls below a threshold via distillation from earlier layers. At inference, a controller picks an offload depth to meet a compute budget, withdraws vision tokens when auditors certify sufficiency, and retains a compact sketch for reversible re-injection when uncertainty spikes, achieving larger speedups than static withdrawal while preserving accuracy. This bridges discrete semantic tokenization with adaptive compute, enabling budget-conditioned, instance-adaptive visual processing in multimodal LLMs.

args.text: We propose Control-Consistent Masked Pretraining (CCMP), a transformer pretraining scheme to make return- or future-conditioned sequence policies reliable in highly stochastic environments. CCMP combines masked trajectory modeling with a controllable-future latent: a DoC-style encoder infers a future code that retains action-contingent structure while discarding exogenous randomness, and the model learns to reconstruct masked tokens and actions conditioned on this code rather than raw future tokens. At finetuning, a lightweight head maps desired returns or waypoint goals into the controllable-future code, as in future-embedding PDT, enabling consistent return-conditioned control and better compositional reuse than DT or masked-only models. We expect improved few-shot in-context adaptation and robustness on Procgen, MiniHack, and stochastic D4RL, with ablations isolating the controllability constraint and mask patterns.

result.text: The paper tackles detecting training-set backdoor attacks, where poisoned examples cause a learned model to respond to a trigger, and questions whether such examples can be distinguished from benign data. Its key insight is that without prior structural knowledge of the data distribution, backdoor patterns can be indistinguishable from legitimate predictive features—making general-purpose detection impossible—and thus defenses implicitly rely on latent assumptions. Leveraging an alternative, explicit assumption that the backdoor corresponds to the single strongest feature in the training data, the authors formalize this setting and derive a detection primitive and algorithm with theoretical guarantees. Empirically, this method proves effective, and the analysis clarifies which assumptions underpin prior defenses and when they succeed or fail.

args.text: Hierarchical Prompt-Sweep Diffusion Prototypes (Hi-PSDP) for open-vocabulary segmentation. We generate multi-granularity candidate masks by sweeping prompts over mined hyponym–hypernym and part-of variants and extracting cross-/self-attention correspondences from a pre-trained diffusion model, yielding coarse, object, and part-level regions. A HIPIE-style decoupled things/stuff head is trained with cross-level consistency, while non-learnable prototypes from CLIP image/text features and diffusion features anchor group tokens at each granularity via contrastive regularization. By aligning diffusion’s intrinsic pixel semantics with language across levels, Hi-PSDP should improve zero-shot hierarchical segmentation and transfer to domain-specific datasets.

We propose Token-Topology-Conditioned Positional Encoding (TT-PE) for dynamic-token Vision Transformers: a lightweight generator that produces positional encodings conditioned on the current set of active tokens, their merged areas, and summaries of dropped tokens. Unlike fixed or globally learned PEs, TT-PE ingests the token mask, original grid coordinates, and low-rank sketches of pruned regions to yield encodings that preserve relative geometry when tokens are pruned or merged, stabilizing attention under large token-count variations. Integrated with pruning/selection and slow–fast updating, and with token merging, TT-PE assigns area-aware encodings to merged tokens and neighborhood-aware corrections to kept tokens, improving accuracy and dense-task transfer at high sparsity. Training adds a PE-consistency regularizer between full-grid and dynamic-grid passes to encourage invariance to token-topology changes.

result.text: The paper studies the effect of gradient clipping—rescaling gradients whose norm exceeds a threshold c—on optimization, addressing gaps in prior convergence analyses that required special c choices or strong noise assumptions. The key insight is that clipping has limited impact in deterministic gradient descent (it only alters higher-order terms) but introduces a stochastic bias that can prevent convergence to the true optimum under standard noise models, so guarantees must explicitly depend on c and the noise structure. Methodologically, the authors derive tight upper and lower bounds for the convergence of the gradient norm for clipped SGD across arbitrary clipping thresholds, proving that deterministic guarantees are robust to clipping while stochastic settings admit unavoidable bias, and corroborate these theoretical findings with experiments.

result.text: The paper addresses the quadratic memory and compute bottleneck of standard Transformer attention that prevents scaling to long sequences. Its key insight is that a carefully designed sparse attention pattern—combining local sliding windows, random global connections, and a small set of global tokens—retains the representational power of full attention (universal approximation and Turing completeness) while reducing complexity from quadratic to linear. The method, BigBird, implements this sparse attention in a Transformer architecture, proves theoretical guarantees about expressivity, and empirically demonstrates the ability to process sequences up to eight times longer than prior models on the same hardware, yielding large gains on long-context NLP tasks (e.g., QA, summarization) and enabling applications like genomics.

result.text: The paper addresses why existing causal representation learning methods fail to disentangle latent factors from multi-object observations, showing that the common assumptions of vector-valued latents and an injective generative map break down when scenes contain multiple interchangeable objects. The key insight is that object-centric inductive biases restore identifiability because representing each object with its own slot makes the generative mapping effectively injective over object properties, so sparse perturbations targeted to objects provide much stronger supervision for causal disentanglement than global Euclidean encodings. Methodologically, the authors modify the Slot Attention architecture to produce object-wise representations and train it with weak supervision from sparse interventions (perturbations) so that each slot learns disentangled properties; empirically this object-centric approach disentangles object attributes with far fewer perturbations than a comparable monolithic encoder in image-based experiments.

Its key insight is that explicitly modeling a hierarchical representation spanning different semantic levels and treating “things” (countable objects) and “stuff” (amorphous regions) differently reduces ambiguity and improves generalization to novel labels. The method, called HIPIE, implements a decoupled text–image fusion and separate representation learning modules for things and stuff, systematically analyzing and adapting to their differing visual and textual feature characteristics, and integrates these components into a unified hierarchical open‑vocabulary segmentation framework. Evaluated across 40+ datasets covering semantic, instance, part, and referring tasks, HIPIE achieves state‑of‑the‑art results.

result.text: The paper tackles the inefficiency of Vision Transformers (ViT) that use a fixed, dense grid of image patches (tokens) for every input, noting that many images are "easy" and don't require high token density while a few "hard" images do. The key insight is that token resolution should be dynamic per image: by starting with few coarse tokens and progressively refining only when needed, one can retain accuracy for difficult cases while saving computation on easy ones. The authors implement this as a cascaded Dynamic Transformer that sequentially activates Transformers with increasing token counts and stops inference early when confidence is sufficient, along with feature-reuse and relationship-reuse mechanisms to avoid redundant computation across stages. Experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR datasets show substantial reductions in FLOPs and inference latency with minimal accuracy loss compared to fixed-token baselines.

args.text: We propose AdaQuantile-Clip, a heavy-tail robust first-order framework for variational inequalities and nonconvex minimization over unbounded domains. The method combines a diagonal AdaGrad preconditioner with online, coordinatewise clipping thresholds chosen via robust quantile estimators of preconditioned gradient magnitudes, so that clipping bias is provably dominated by statistical error without knowing the tail index p or noise scale. For SGDA/SEG in monotone and structured non-monotone VIPs we derive high-probability rates with only logarithmic dependence on confidence, and for nonconvex minimization we obtain last-iterate guarantees comparable to normalized/clipped methods, all without bounded-domain assumptions. The analysis explicitly quantifies clipping bias using recent bias bounds for clipping and converts expectation-style guarantees to high-probability via noise-adaptive concentration, extending clipped SEG/SGDA and normalized heavy-tail techniques.

Anchor-KV Synthesis: instead of caching keys/values at every layer during autoregressive decoding, cache them only at sparse anchor layers and reconstruct the missing layers’ KV on-the-fly with tiny per-layer synthesizers conditioned on the nearest anchor cache and the current hidden state. Train with a teacher that uses full KV caches and distill attention logits/weights, while randomizing anchor placements and applying progressive compression to anchor caches to make the model robust across memory budgets. At inference, this yields KV memory scaling with the number of anchors rather than layers, compounding gains from compression and keeping latency low because synthesizers are lightweight adapters. This generalizes cross-layer KV sharing to non-adjacent layers and is expected to enable 8–16× smaller KV memory with minimal quality loss on long-context decoding.

result.text: The paper addresses causal representation learning from high-dimensional temporal observations when real-world sampling rates are too slow to resolve fast causal interactions, creating effective "instantaneous" effects that break prior identifiability results. The key insight is that when interventions (e.g., agent actions) are observable, one can jointly learn a mapping from observations to multidimensional causal variables and a causal graph that permits instantaneous effects, restoring identifiability in intervened sequences. The proposed method, iCITRIS, uses a differentiable encoder to recover latent causal variables from temporal data while concurrently applying a differentiable causal discovery module that models both instantaneous and time-lagged edges conditioned on observed intervention targets; training is end-to-end on sequences with interventions to recover variables and their causal graph.

result.text: The paper tackles the lack of a scalable, promptable 3D segmentation foundation model for point clouds—hampered by fragmented data formats, limited labeled masks, and poor model scalability—by proposing Point-SAM. The key insight is that the rich segmentation knowledge in 2D foundation models (notably SAM) can be distilled into a 3D point-cloud model via large-scale pseudo-label generation, enabling promptable, general-purpose 3D segmentation without massive manual 3D mask annotation. Methodologically, the authors design an efficient transformer-based architecture tailored to point clouds, build a data engine that uses 2D SAM to produce part- and object-level pseudo-labels across many views/frames, and train Point-SAM on this synthetic supervisory signal; the resulting model achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple indoor and outdoor benchmarks and supports interactive annotation and zero-shot instance proposals.

result.text: The paper addresses how to make neural networks perform reinforcement learning entirely in-context—i.e., adapt their policy during deployment without parameter updates—by distilling the dynamics of an RL training process into a sequence model. The key insight is that a causal sequence model can be trained to predict actions conditioned on past interactions from full learning histories, allowing the model to internalize an RL algorithm and execute it at test time by autoregressively interpreting contextual episode data. Methodologically, the authors generate datasets of learning trajectories from a source RL algorithm, train a causal transformer to autoregressively predict next actions given preceding observations, actions, rewards, and other learning-history tokens, and demonstrate that this Algorithm Distillation approach can solve sparse-reward, combinatorial, and pixel-based tasks in-context—often more data-efficiently than the original source learner.

args.text: We propose Audio-Conditioned Cycle-Masked Distillation: an unsupervised pretraining scheme that unifies patch-level cycle-consistent correspondence, asymmetric masked reconstruction, and cross-modal knowledge transfer. We build a space-time patch graph whose transition probabilities are modulated by concurrent audio features so random-walk cycles stay within acoustic events; training jointly maximizes visual cycle-return likelihood, reconstructs heavily masked future-frame patches from a past frame, and distills an audio teacher into the visual student via domain alignment. High-probability cycles are then clustered into segment-level pseudo-labels that supervise a lightweight head, yielding stronger long-range correspondence and temporal segmentation, especially for sound-visible actions. Compared to pure visual cycle learning or generic audio-visual contrast, audio-conditioned walks provide event-aware grouping while masked prediction encourages object-centric features, improving label-free performance on propagation, retrieval, and action segmentation.

result.text: Causal Component Analysis (CauCA) addresses the problem of recovering latent components and their causal mechanisms from observed mixtures when the causal graph among latents is known, bridging Independent Component Analysis (ICA) and Causal Representation Learning (CRL). The key insight is that by assuming the latent causal graph is given and leveraging interventional variation across multiple datasets, one can characterize identifiability conditions for recovering the unmixing function and the causal conditionals—showing that interventions enable recovery in cases where standard ICA or CRL would fail and yielding tighter identifiability for nonlinear ICA as a special case. Methodologically, the authors analyze identifiability under different intervention types and propose a practical likelihood-based estimator using normalizing flows to jointly learn the invertible unmixing map and the parametrized causal mechanisms, validating the approach with synthetic experiments that confirm improved recovery under their theoretical conditions.

result.text: The paper tackles improving transformer-based architectures for 3D point cloud understanding by addressing limitations in the original Point Transformer around attention expressiveness, positional encoding, and inefficient pooling/sampling. Its key insight is that replacing the original vector attention with a grouped vector attention—combining multi-head structure with learnable grouped weight encodings and an added position-encoding multiplier—yields richer, more stable local feature interactions, while partition-based pooling provides better spatial alignment and efficiency than naive sampling. Methodologically, the authors introduce a grouped weight encoding layer and implement grouped vector attention with a position encoding multiplier, and design lightweight partition-based pooling schemes to aggregate local features and sample points more effectively; together these changes form Point Transformer V2, which outperforms prior models on segmentation and classification benchmarks.

args.text: We propose Deletion-Smoothing Certified Unlearning: maintain an ensemble of base learners trained on random sub-bags and serve predictions by majority vote, while processing unlearning requests by efficiently removing or down-weighting affected examples in each base model using cached sufficient statistics or influence-function approximations, avoiding full retraining. We derive instance-wise certificates that, given the vote margin and the inclusion counts of training points across sub-bags, bound the maximum number of deletions (in any static or adaptive sequence) that cannot flip a specific prediction via a tight counting argument analogous to bagging-based poisoning certificates. This design directly resists unlearning-triggered backdoors and sequential manipulation by forcing an attacker to simultaneously sway many independent submodels, and it mitigates denial-of-service by bounding per-request update time. We will evaluate certified accuracy–time trade-offs against recent unlearning-induced backdoor and sequential manipulation attacks and report per-example certified deletion budgets.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of learning text-supervised semantic segmentation without relying on dense human annotations, specifically addressing the gap that prior methods ignore correspondence among multiple augmented views of the same image. The key insight is that enforcing multi-view semantic consistency—both by aligning each view with the same text supervision (text-to-views consistency) and by contrasting segment-level features across Siamese visual encoder views (cross-view segmentation consistency)—reduces ambiguity in text labels and yields denser, more stable segment assignments. Methodologically, ViewCo trains on large-scale image–text data using a dual mechanism: it encourages different crops to match the same text embedding to distribute semantic labels across views, and it applies a cross-view contrastive loss on segment features to provide self-supervision for mask consistency; this combination enables zero-shot segmentation of arbitrary categories and improves mIoU on PASCAL VOC2012, PASCAL Context, and COCO.

result.text: The paper tackles multi-label temporal action detection, where multiple, potentially overlapping action classes must be precisely localized within untrimmed videos—a setting that requires fine-grained class discrimination and accurate boundary localization beyond conventional single-label TAD benchmarks. The key insight is to represent each action instance not by dense segments but by a small set of learnable query points that can flexibly attend to discriminative frames at boundaries and inside actions, enabling better differentiation of co-occurring events. Methodologically, PointTAD extends sparse query-based detection to the multi-label setting by learning per-instance query points and decoding actions with a Multi-level Interactive Module that integrates point-level and instance-level semantics in an end-to-end RGB-only framework, and is evaluated using a new detection-mAP metric where it substantially outperforms prior methods.

The paper challenges the common assumption that vision architectures require a locality inductive bias by showing that vanilla Transformers treating each individual pixel as a token can perform competitively across multiple vision tasks. The key insight is that per-pixel tokenization—eschewing the 16×16 patch aggregation used in Vision Transformers—still allows the model to learn effective image representations for supervised classification/regression, masked autoencoding self-supervision, and diffusion-based image generation. Methodologically, the authors simply apply standard Transformer architectures to sequences of pixel tokens (with appropriate positional embeddings and comparable training setups) and compare performance to patch-based counterparts, demonstrating surprisingly strong results despite higher computational cost. This finding suggests that locality priors like patching are not strictly necessary for high performance, prompting reconsideration of architectural biases in future vision models.

result.text: The paper tackles weakly-supervised semantic segmentation with only image-level labels, where classifier-based localization maps tend to focus on sparse discriminative object parts and thus produce poor pseudo-labels for segmentation. The key insight is to intentionally suppress the most discriminative activations so the model is encouraged to shift attention to adjacent, non-discriminative regions, producing denser and more complete localization maps. They implement this as a lightweight Discriminative Region Suppression (DRS) module that can be plugged into existing networks with few or no extra parameters, and pair it with a localization map refinement learning strategy that iteratively enhances maps by recovering missing parts and removing noise. Together these simple components yield substantially improved pseudo-labels and segmentation performance, achieving 71.4% mIoU on PASCAL VOC 2012 using only image-level supervision.

result.text: The paper tackles the high computational and memory cost of training Transformers on long sequences by reducing attention and activation-storage bottlenecks. The key insight is that attention can be approximated with locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) to limit pairwise comparisons and that reversible residual layers eliminate the need to store intermediate activations for every layer. The method implements LSH-based attention to reduce attention complexity from O(L^2) to O(L log L) and replaces standard residual connections with reversible functions so activations are recomputed during the backward pass, yielding the Reformer architecture. Empirically, Reformers match standard Transformer performance while using far less memory and running much faster on long-sequence tasks.

The key insight is that, under mild mathematical conditions, the decoder’s three sub-layers (self-attention, encoder–decoder attention, and feed-forward) can be algebraically combined or compressed into a single equivalent sub-layer, enabling more parallel computation without degrading representational power. result.text: The paper addresses unsupervised 3D object segmentation from raw point clouds, aiming to discover and segment multiple rigid objects without any human annotations. The key insight is that rigid objects induce consistent dynamic motion patterns across sequential point clouds, which can be exploited as self-supervision to reveal object geometry and boundaries. The OGC method combines a single-frame object segmentation network, an auxiliary self-supervised scene flow estimator, and a core object geometry consistency module, training with losses that enforce multi-object rigid consistency and shape invariance across space and time. Evaluated on five indoor and outdoor datasets, OGC demonstrates strong performance on object part instance segmentation and general object segmentation without labeled data.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of producing post-hoc explanations for black-box classifiers that are causal—i.e., interventions on explanatory factors change the classifier’s outputs—without requiring labeled attributes or prior causal structure. The key insight is to learn a low-dimensional latent representation via a generative model whose latent factors are optimized not only to reconstruct the data distribution but also to have high causal influence on the classifier’s output, measured with information-theoretic criteria. The method jointly trains a generative model (e.g., VAE/GAN-style) and a causal objective that quantifies how interventions on latent dimensions alter predicted class probabilities, yielding interpretable global and local factors; it works with any differentiable classifier that provides class probabilities and gradients and is validated on controlled examples and image recognition tasks.

args.text: We propose Prompt-aware Prototypical Panoptic (PPP), a 3D point-cloud model that fuses promptable foundation knowledge with a unified prototype-based view of semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation. PPP tokenizes local point patches and projects them through a frozen CLIP transformer to obtain features, then distills large-scale 2D SAM-derived pseudo-masks into a global 3D prototype bank that spans parts, objects, and scenes. At inference, text and click prompts select or compose subsets of prototypes to condition a fixed set of instance queries whose classifier weights are initialized from the chosen prototypes and optimized via bipartite matching, producing panoptic masks without heuristic grouping. This yields controllable, zero-shot-capable panoptic segmentation while retaining strong supervised performance across tasks with a single, transparent prototype space.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of generative modeling for decision-making tasks where actions are continuous, multimodal, and must be predicted sequentially without error compounding, a setting where prior discretization-based Behavior Transformers (BeT) struggle due to k-means’ scaling and lack of gradient information. The key insight is that hierarchical vector quantization can more effectively tokenize high-dimensional continuous actions into discrete latent codes that preserve multimodal structure and are learnable end-to-end, enabling richer long-range action modeling. The proposed method, VQ-BeT, augments the transformer-based behavior model with a hierarchical VQ module that converts continuous actions into discrete tokens for sequence modeling, supporting conditional generation and partial observations; across seven diverse environments it outperforms BeT and diffusion-policy baselines while capturing behavior modes better and running inference about five times faster than diffusion methods.

result.text: The paper addresses learning rich self-supervised video representations from unlabelled audio-visual data, aiming to capture both modality-specific features and complementary cross-modal information despite domain discrepancies between audio and visual streams. The key insight is that combining masked-data reconstruction to learn strong modality-specific embeddings with a self-supervised teacher–student cross-modal knowledge distillation, augmented by a domain alignment strategy, enables effective transfer of complementary cues across modalities. The method trains two pseudo-objectives: (1) masked reconstruction on audio and visual inputs to build modality-tailored encoders, and (2) cross-modal knowledge distillation where a teacher from one modality guides a student in the other after aligning their feature domains, and it also proposes modality-agnostic variants that reuse a single pretrained backbone for both streams. Empirically, XKD yields substantial gains on action and sound classification benchmarks (e.g., +8–14% on UCF101/HMDB51/Kinetics400, +5.5% multimodal on Kinetics-Sound, and 96.5% on ESC50).
